notes: Pennsylvania taxes eight separate classes of income at a flat 3.07%; it has no standard deduction or personal exemption. Business income is PA net profit from PA-40 Schedule C, figured under PA rules rather than federal AGI.
Losses in one income class cannot offset income in another class (e.g., a business loss cannot offset wages); not modeled.
Tax Forgiveness credit (PA-40 Schedule SP) can eliminate or reduce tax for low-income households based on eligibility income and family size; not modeled.
PA allows a few deductions on Schedule O (e.g., HSA and Archer MSA contributions, PA 529 contributions); not modeled.
Married couples filing jointly are taxed at the same flat rate, so filing status does not change the rate.

seDeduction.note: The PA Personal Income Tax Guide states the one-half of self-employment tax the IRS allows may not be deducted for Pennsylvania purposes.

seHealthInsurance.note: PA-40 Schedule C instructions say you may not deduct payments for your own personal coverage; Pennsylvania has no self-employed health insurance deduction.

retirementContributions.note: A self-employed person's contributions to his or her own pension plan (SEP, Keogh/solo 401(k), IRA) are not deductible in figuring PA net profits; only contributions for employees are.

qbi.note: Pennsylvania does not start from federal income and has no QBI deduction.

localIncomeTax.note: Nearly every Pennsylvania municipality and school district levies a local Earned Income Tax (EIT) on residents' wages and net profits under Act 511/Act 32. The combined resident rate is usually 1% (statutory default cap split between municipality and school district) but is higher in many places (Act 50 school districts up to 1.5%, Pittsburgh School District up to 2%, and home-rule municipalities are not bound by the cap). Philadelphia residents instead pay the city's Net Profits Tax: 3.735% for tax year 2026 (3.425% non-residents); Philadelphia also imposes the Business Income and Receipts Tax (1.395 mills on gross receipts + 5.65% of net income for 2026, with no $100,000 exemption since 2025; 60% of the net-income portion is credited against Net Profits Tax). Choose Philadelphia in the calculator to include both. A flat Local Services Tax may also apply where you work. Look up your exact rate with DCED's Act 32 address search.

localities.note: Replaces the 1% earned income tax used for the rest of Pennsylvania. 2026 resident rates: Net Profits Tax 3.735% of net profits; BIRT 1.395 mills on gross receipts plus 5.65% of net income, with 60% of the net-income portion credited against Net Profits Tax. The $100,000 BIRT exemption no longer applies. Wage Tax is 3.74% until June 30, 2026 and 3.735% after; 3.735% is used for the year.

estimatedTax.threshold: Required if you expect to owe at least $430 of PA tax after withholding and credits for 2026 (i.e., $14,000 or more of income not subject to withholding).
estimatedTax.safeHarbor: No underpayment penalty if timely withholding, credits and estimated payments are at least the smaller of 90% of the 2026 tax or 100% of 2025 net PA taxable income multiplied by 3.07% (full-year 2025 PA-40 filers only).
estimatedTax.form: PA-40 ES (I) declaration voucher with REV-414 (I) worksheet (or pay online via myPATH)

businessCosts.llcFormationFee: $125 Certificate of Organization (Pennsylvania Department of State).
businessCosts.annualReportFee: $7 annual report for for-profit LLCs, due every year by September 30 (required since 2025).
businessCosts.franchiseOrMinimumTax: None. Pennsylvania imposes no franchise, capital stock or minimum tax on sole proprietors or single-member LLCs taxed as disregarded entities.
businessCosts.grossReceiptsTax: None statewide for typical freelancers. Philadelphia's Business Income and Receipts Tax (BIRT) applies to businesses operating in Philadelphia (2026: 1.395 mills on gross receipts plus 5.65% of net income; the $100,000 exemption no longer applies, and 60% of the net-income portion is credited against Net Profits Tax).
